dedupe_keys.name: gsma intelligence consumer survey and mobile gender gap report

description: The GSMA Consumer Survey is a yearly nationally representative, face-to-face survey of mobile phone ownership and use in low- and middle-income countries, run by GSMA Intelligence for the GSMA's Connected Women programme and reported each year in the Mobile Gender Gap Report. It measures who owns a mobile phone or smartphone, who uses mobile internet and how often, what they use it for, and what stops non-users, such as handset cost, literacy and digital skills, safety and security concerns and relevance, broken down by sex, age, education, income and rural or urban residence. The 2024 report drew on more than 13,600 interviews in 12 countries and found that women were 15 per cent less likely than men to use mobile internet and that the smartphone ownership gap was 14 per cent; rural people were 28 per cent less likely to use mobile internet than urban people. Coverage: about 12 low- and middle-income countries each year in Africa, Asia and Latin America, reports since 2018. Format and access: reports and country figures free on the GSMA website; core survey data on request from the Connected Women team, with no open licence. Caveats: countries change between waves; self-reported use; microdata are not openly published. Simulation uses: behavioural and equity parameters for agent-based models of mobile service use, and identifying groups most affected by network outages. Related records: the ITU ICT statistics and national internet use surveys such as the NTIA and Statistics Canada ones cover use in other countries.
